I'll work through each draft chapter carefully, applying the five tests and gate test to every potentially damaged sentence.

---

**Ch 030 draft scan**

- "What, perhaps, made Stubb such an easy-going, unfearing man, that thing must have been his pipe." — The source has "what, perhaps, with other things, made Stubb such an easy-going, unfearing man…what helped to bring about that almost impious good-humor of his; that thing must have been his pipe." The draft's truncation is grammatically awkward but the main clause ("that thing must have been his pipe") still parses and the reader understands the pipe is being credited. Not a structural failure.
- "They called him King-Post on board the Pequod; because, in form, he could be likened to the short, square timber known by that name in Arctic whalers." — Source adds a gloss explaining what the King-Post timber does (braces the ship against icy concussions). But the draft tells the reader what King-Post is (a timber in Arctic whalers) and the nickname's basis (Flask's form resembles it). The dropped functional explanation is atmospheric ornamentation; the reader knows what King-Post refers to. Not a finding.
- "Each mate or headsman, like a Gothic Knight of old, is always accompanied by his boat-steerer or harpooneer." — Source continues this into the reason for introducing the harpooneers ("it is therefore but meet, that in this place we set down who the Pequod's harpooneers were"). The draft cuts this bridge sentence but immediately proceeds to list the harpooneers; the transition is slightly abrupt but fully parseable. Not a finding.
- "Elijah's diabolical incoherences" in Ch 031 draft — Elijah is an authorized minor-character removal. The reference survives in the draft but Elijah was never introduced in the draft. Check below.

**Ch 031 draft scan**

- "strangely heightened by Elijah's diabolical incoherences uninvitedly recurring to me" — Elijah is in the authorized removal list. But the source reference to Elijah occurs in Ch 031's own source text (not in a removed chapter passage surviving into this chapter). The drafter chose to keep this clause rather than cut it. Since Elijah has been removed as a character and never appears in any surviving draft passage, a reader of the draft has no referent for "Elijah." This is a dangling reference to a character whose introduction was in an authorized-cut chapter, but the drafter's decision to *retain* this reference (rather than cut the clause as well) creates the seam. The question is whether this is a "direct residue of an authorized cut" and thus expected/not-a-finding, or whether it is a compression error in material that should have survived. Since Elijah is an authorized removal, the dangling reference is an expected seam — NOT a finding per the rules.

- "A grey Manxman, an old sepulchral man popularly invested with preternatural powers of discernment, insinuated that if ever Captain Ahab should be tranquilly laid out, whoever should do that last office for the dead, would find a birth-mark on him from crown to sole." — The source introduces this Manxman's claim as a counter to Tashtego's senior's claim (that the mark came upon Ahab at forty in an elemental strife at sea). The source structure is: Tashtego's senior asserts X → but the Manxman insinuated Y (which "inferentially negatived" X). The draft cuts Tashtego's senior entirely (authorized removal) and presents only the Manxman's insinuation, stripped of its "yet/however" pivot. The Old Manxman is also an authorized removal. This is a direct residue of authorized cuts. NOT a finding.

- "This ivory leg had at sea been fashioned from the polished bone of the sperm whale's jaw." — In the source, this fact is introduced with "It had previously come to me that this ivory leg…" establishing that Ishmael already knew this. The draft presents it as a flat statement with no issue of parseability. Structurally fine.

- "said an old Gay-Head Indian" — In the source this is "said the old Gay-Head Indian once" — referring to Tashtego's senior, who is an authorized removal. The draft strips the definite article to "an old Gay-Head Indian," which is a reasonable adjustment. Not a finding.

---

After exhaustive review, no sentence in either draft chapter fails any of the five structural tests in a way that is not either (a) a residue of an authorized cut, or (b) merely a less-ornamented version of the source.
